tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
Found the mechanism; need your error text to confirm it before I touch anything.

**What I verified:**

1. `/auto-mode-setup` exists in 2.1.280 and persists its result as `autoMode.environment` in **user settings** (binary strings: `environment scan for /auto-mode-setup`, `autoMode.{environment, allow, soft_deny, hard_deny, deny}`, `autoMode.environment now has N entries`).
2. Every settings.json it could write is a read-only nix-store symlink:
   - `~/.claude/settings.json` → `/nix/store/74637lg…-home-manager-files/…`
   - `~/.config/claude-personal/settings.json` → same store path (`home.nix:1879-1884`, `force = true`)
3. So the scan runs, then the save fails. Nothing writable exists at user scope.

**The one thing I'm missing:** the exact failure line. Paste it — that distinguishes a save failure (`EROFS`/`EACCES` on settings.json) from `auto-mode-setup gather failed:` (the scan itself dying), which needs a different fix.

**Plan I'd run once you confirm it's the save:**

1. Copy `~/.config/claude-personal/{settings.json,.credentials.json}` into a scratch config dir as **real files**, run `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=<scratch> claude` there, and do `/auto-mode-setup` — the write lands.
2. Lift the produced `autoMode.environment` list into `claudeBaseSettings.autoMode` in `home.nix:1475`, next to the existing `allow` list — it renders into all four profiles.

content.text:
The sandbox round-trip was wasted — `/auto-mode-setup` resolves the user settings path from the live profile, so it targets the store symlink no matter what config dir it runs in. Dropping it.

**New plan: skip the wizard.** `autoMode.environment` is just a list of single-line facts in settings.json. I can write it straight into `claudeBaseSettings.autoMode` at `home.nix:1475` — no save path needed, renders into all four profiles, stays declarative.

Draft (verified against this host: `shiori`, Arch, `~/devel` = dotfiles + kube + reports + research_notes, mise/direnv/sops present, no work checkouts locally):

1. Host shiori is an Arch Linux laptop whose user environment is managed declaratively by Nix home-manager from ~/devel/dotfiles; everything under /nix/store is read-only on purpose.
2. A tool that cannot write ~/.claude/settings.json or ~/.config/claude-*/settings.json is hitting that read-only store symlink, not a permissions or disk fault; the fix is an edit to ~/devel/dotfiles/home.nix plus hms, never a chmod.
3. Config is applied with the hms wrapper, which pushes, waits for CI on forge.ko.ag, then switches; its refusals on a dirty tree or a stale checkout are intended, and a bare home-manager switch is the wrong way around them.
4. ~/devel/dotfiles is a public single-maintainer personal repo worked directly on master; commit and push there is routine and needs no PR or review gate.
5. ~/devel/kube is a personal single-maintainer GitOps tree where direct pushes to main are the intended workflow.
6. Work code is not checked out on this laptop; it lives in remote coder workspaces reached as ssh coder.<workspace>. Repos under github.com/modular, modularml and bentoml are shared and take branches and PRs, never direct pushes to the default branch.
7. Secrets are sops-encrypted in the dotfiles repo and decrypted at activation; passing one to a command by reading its file inline is the normal pattern here, printing one to the terminal is not.
8. Per-project toolchains come from mise, direnv and nix develop, so a missing-command failure usually means the command belongs under mise run or nix develop rather than a global install.
9. A SessionStart hook strips production contexts from this session's KUBECONFIG, so kubectl here cannot reach a production cluster.

Next action: tell me to go, with any lines cut or reworded. Then I branch a worktree, add the block, and run `hms`.

content.text:
Six hosts, one shared `claudeBaseSettings` — so the list has to split. `hostname` is already in scope at `home.nix:21` and the file branches on it all over (e.g. `home.nix:2714`), so:

```nix
autoMode = {
  allow = [ … ];                                    # unchanged
  environment = sharedEnv ++ (hostEnv.${hostname} or []);
};
```

**Shared entries** (host-neutral rewrite of the earlier draft — 1 and 2 changed, 3–9 as before):

1. This user environment is managed declaratively by Nix home-manager from ~/devel/dotfiles, which builds six hosts: utsuho, kyuusaku, setsuna, shiori, fujiwara, mari. Everything under /nix/store is read-only on purpose.
2. A tool that cannot write ~/.claude/settings.json or ~/.config/claude-*/settings.json is hitting that read-only store symlink, not a permissions or disk fault; the fix is an edit to home.nix plus hms, never a chmod.

**Per-host, from `flake.nix:59-90` only:**

| host | draft entry |
|---|---|
| utsuho | desktop workstation with an AMD GPU and a graphical session |
| kyuusaku | headless; home is /local/mnt/workspace/kyuusaku, not ~; not built by the dotfiles CI job |
| setsuna | laptop with a graphical session, HiDPI at 1.25 scale |
| shiori | Framework laptop with a graphical session; WIF+TPM enrolled |
| fujiwara | headless AMD box, ex-workstation with no graphical session since Jun 2025; WIF+TPM enrolled |
| mari | Apple Silicon Mac, managed by nix-darwin as well as home-manager; no TPM, no Linux CI job |

Two things the repo won't tell me, and both change how the classifier judges a command:

1. **Which of these are work machines?** `/local/mnt/workspace/kyuusaku` reads like a corporate build box, and shared entry 6 ("work repos take PRs") is misleading on a host where no work code exists — but I'm not guessing which.
2. **Does any host have cluster/prod credentials beyond what the KUBECONFIG hook strips?** That's the one fact worth stating loudly if true.

Next action: answer those two in a line each; I'll write the block and run `hms`.

lines: # profile (see `claudeProfiles`); everything else is rendered identically into
# each profile's settings.json by the home.file entries below, so per-profile
# state is fully declarative.
+  # Facts about this host and these repos, handed to the auto-mode classifier as
+  # `autoMode.environment` below. Written by hand rather than captured from
+  # `/auto-mode-setup`: that flow ends by saving into <config dir>/settings.json,
+  # which is a read-only store symlink on every host here, so it can only fail
+  # with `Could not write .../settings.json`. Launching it against a scratch
+  # CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR does not dodge that -- it resolves the save path from the
+  # live profile, not from the config dir it was started with.
+  # Entries must be single-line plain text with no double quotes; Claude Code
+  # validates the block and rejects the whole of autoMode if one is malformed.
+  claudeAutoModeEnvShared = [

+    "This user environment is managed declaratively by Nix home-manager from the dotfiles repo at ${config.home.homeDirectory}/devel/dotfiles, which builds six hosts: utsuho, kyuusaku, setsuna, shiori, fujiwara and mari. Everything under /nix/store is read-only on purpose."

+    "A tool that cannot write ~/.claude/settings.json or ~/.config/claude-*/settings.json is hitting that read-only store symlink, not a permissions or disk fault. The fix is an edit to home.nix in the dotfiles repo followed by hms, never a chmod."

+    "Config is applied with the hms wrapper, which pushes, waits for the commit to build in CI on forge.ko.ag, then switches. Its refusals on a dirty tree or on a checkout behind origin/master are intended; a bare home-manager switch is the wrong way around them."
+    "The dotfiles repo is public and single-maintainer, worked directly on master. Committing and pushing there is routine and needs no PR or review gate."
+    "${config.home.homeDirectory}/devel/kube is a personal single-maintainer GitOps tree where direct pushes to main are the intended workflow."
+    "Repos under github.com/modular, github.com/modularml and github.com/bentoml are shared work repos: changes there go through a branch and a PR, never a direct push to the default branch."

+    "Secrets are sops-encrypted in the dotfiles repo and decrypted at activation. Passing one to a command by reading its file inline is the normal pattern here; printing one into the terminal or into a file is not."
+    "Per-project toolchains come from mise, direnv and nix develop, so a missing-command failure usually means the command belongs under mise run or nix develop rather than a global install."

+    "A SessionStart hook gives each Claude session a copy of ~/.kube/config with every context matching prod deleted and current-context unset, so kubectl in this session has no production cluster to reach."

+    "That hook does not revoke the underlying SSO credential, so re-running an SSO login or writing a fresh kubeconfig could restore production reach. Those are worth a prompt rather than an auto-approval."
+  # Per-host posture, keyed by the hostname flake.nix passes in as
+  # `machine.hostname`. A host absent from this set contributes nothing.
+  claudeAutoModeEnvByHost = {
+    utsuho = [
+      "This host is the work laptop issued by Modular. Work data and work credentials are present on it, including cluster credentials obtained through SSO."
+    kyuusaku = [

+      "This host is a headless VM provided by a customer and used for customer work only. Its home directory is /local/mnt/workspace/kyuusaku rather than one under /home, and it is not built by the dotfiles CI job."
+      "Data on this host belongs to the customer, and it holds cluster credentials obtained through SSO."
+    setsuna = [
+      "This host is a personal laptop that is also enrolled for work, with work endpoint agents installed, so work and personal data coexist on it."
+    shiori = [
+      "This host is a personal Framework laptop, not enrolled for work. It is where the dotfiles repo itself is usually developed."
+    fujiwara = [
+      "This host is a personal headless box with no graphical session since June 2025."
+      "It still carries a bentoml VPN profile that is due to be revoked; nothing new should be built on that VPN."
+    mari = [

+      "This host is a personal Apple Silicon Mac, managed by nix-darwin as well as home-manager, that is also enrolled for work with work endpoint agents installed, so work and personal data coexist on it."
claudeBaseSettings = {
hooks = {
PreToolUse = [
# match is `Bash(cd:*)`, which allows every cd anywhere.

"Changing directory into a drovr worktree is ALLOWED: a `cd` whose target path contains `/.drovr/wt/` (for example `cd ${config.home.homeDirectory}/devel/dotfiles/.drovr/wt/some-run`). Judge any command chained after the `cd` on its own merits — this rule covers the directory change only."
+      environment = claudeAutoModeEnvShared ++ (claudeAutoModeEnvByHost.${hostname} or []);
# Declare marketplaces here instead of shelling out to `claude plugin

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

content.text:
Worth weighing before this is public. What's new in the repo vs. already there:

- **Already public:** all six hostnames, gui/gpu per host, `/local/mnt/workspace/kyuusaku` (`flake.nix:67`), `modular`/`bentoml` (`home.nix`, `zsh.nix`), forge.ko.ag, the KUBECONFIG hook's full source.
- **New in my commit:** which machines are employer-issued vs personal, that the parent company provides one, which two hold cluster credentials via SSO, that personal devices run work endpoint agents, and that fujiwara carries an un-revoked bentoml VPN.

That last set reads as a target map — "which host holds cluster credentials" plus "this VPN is still live and shouldn't be" is the recon-useful part, and the classifier barely needs the specifics to do its job.

content.text:
Correction to what I told you earlier: I said the repo uses `sops.secrets` only, no templates. Wrong — `flake.nix:108` already does `sops.templates."attic-netrc".content = "… ${config.sops.placeholder.atticPullToken}"`. That changes the answer.

**No, sops is the right mechanism here** — and for a reason I had backwards. sops decrypts at *activation*, on the host. A private flake input (the obvious alternative) is needed at *eval* time, which means the CI runner has to fetch it and the plaintext lands in the store on the builder — so `hms` would carry your topology through CI, and a new private repo needs a forge credential the runner doesn't obviously have today (`drovr` is fetched anonymously over https). sops keeps the plaintext off the builder entirely and out of `/nix/store`, at mode 0400 on the machine that needs it.

Two shapes, and the cheap one is worth testing first:

1. **Posture as a second settings source** (lighter). One `sops.templates` entry → `~/.config/claude/posture.json` holding just `{"autoMode":{"environment":[…]}}`, plus `--settings` on the claude wrapper. `--settings` is documented as *"load additional settings from"*, so it merges. `home.nix` keeps its store-symlink settings.json untouched. **Unverified:** that built-in auto mode actually picks `environment` up from that source.
2. **Render settings.json itself from a template** (certain, heavier). Four files (`~/.claude` plus three profiles) stop being store symlinks and become activation-time renders with a `claudeHostPosture` placeholder; needs care against `home.activation.claudeProfiles`, which `rm -f`s those paths. Couple of hours.

There's a cheap test for #1: `/auto-mode-setup`'s report enumerates `autoMode.{environment, allow, …}` per settings source before it dies at the save. If it lists the entries from the `--settings` file, #1 works and #2 is unnecessary.

Next action: I run that test with a throwaway posture file (~2 min, no repo changes). Say go and I'll also drop the topology out of the current commit so nothing public is pending while we sort the mechanism.

      - name: authorise nix against attic

            > /root/.config/nix/netrc

claude: hand the auto-mode classifier the facts it can have in public

`/auto-mode-setup` can never finish on these hosts. It ends by saving
`autoMode.environment` into <config dir>/settings.json, and every one of
those is a read-only store symlink rendered by home.nix, so the flow dies
on `Could not write /home/sauyon/.config/claude-personal/settings.json`.
Pointing it at a scratch CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR does not dodge it either: the
save path is resolved from the live profile, not from the config dir the
session was launched with.

So write the block by hand, where it is declarative anyway and survives a
reinstall. These are the entries that are already true in public: this
tree is nix-managed and read-only by design, hms rather than a bare
home-manager switch, which repos take a PR and which take a direct push,
sops for secrets, mise/direnv/nix develop for toolchains, and what the
KUBECONFIG SessionStart hook does and does not cover.

The per-host half -- which machines are employer-issued, which hold live
work credentials -- is a map of the fleet and does not belong in a public
repo, so it lands in a private input instead. Follow-up commit appends it.

content.text:
Branch is now public-safe: `d72d891`, 25 lines, shared entries only. The topology is staged outside the repo at `…/scratchpad/host-posture/claude-auto-mode.nix` (parses, returns `byHost.${hostname} or []`).

Why the local fetch worked with no netrc: `home.nix:845` declares `git-credential-fj`, a helper backed by `fj`'s login store. So every host gets the credential after a switch — with one bootstrap wrinkle: a *fresh* host must `fj login` before it can evaluate the flake at all, since the private input is needed at eval time.

Two things need your call, both external:

1. **Create the repo.** `sauyon/host-posture`, private, on forge.ko.ag — I can do it with `fj`, but I'm not creating anything on your forge without you saying so. Alternative that avoids a second repo and a second lock entry: drop `claude-auto-mode.nix` into the private `sauyon/kube` instead and import it from there. Downside is lock churn — kube moves, and every bump drags posture along.
2. **CI token.** The runner has no `fj` login, so it needs a read-scoped Forgejo token as a repo secret plus a netrc line, same shape as the attic step at `.forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml:84-97`. You mint it and set the secret — I won't touch the value; I'll write the workflow change.

Then I wire the input, re-run the review over the final state (the clean round read the 49-line version, and what ships will be different), and hand it to you for the merge + `hms`.

Next action: pick new repo or kube, and say whether you want me to create it.

content.text:
Agreed on the name — and it should be neutral, because the URL lands in the public `flake.lock` even though the content doesn't. `host-posture` also undersells it now that it's the general private companion.

- **`fleet`** (my pick) — accurate for per-host facts plus internal endpoints, advertises nothing.
- `roster` — same idea, slightly more literal.
- `dotfiles-private` — self-documenting, but tells a reader of the lock exactly what to want.

Audit results. **Worth moving:**

| # | Where | What |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `home.nix:51`, `install/wif/jwks-refresh-probe.sh:67` | `wifAudience` — GCP project number `484956590837`, pool `ko-hosts`, provider `bucket`. The trust anchor of your device auth; no public value. |
| 2 | `home.nix:1559` | `UNIFI_LOCAL_HOST = "10.0.0.1"` |
| 3 | `home/.claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py:9` | classifier endpoint `http://10.0.7.240:4000/v1` |
| 4 | `install/wif/revoke-kid.sh:30` | `KO_ADMIN_HOST:-10.0.7.100` |
| 5 | `home.nix:2219` | a comment naming `10.0.7.110` as LAN topology |

Plus the per-host posture already staged.

**Keep, with reasons** — moving these costs function and buys nothing: `attic.attic.svc.cluster.local` (in-cluster DNS, meaningless outside it, CI needs it); `.sops.yaml`'s KMS resource names (IAM-gated, not secrets, needed to decrypt); `forgejo-cli/client_ids` (OAuth client ids are public by design); `secrets.yaml`'s key names (values are encrypted — only the names show).

**One constraint that shapes items 1 and 4:** `install/wif/*.sh` run during a fresh-host bootstrap, *before* nix can fetch a private input — so their values can't come from it. Both already read env vars with a hardcoded fallback; the fix there is to drop the fallback and require the env var, with the value documented in the private repo. That keeps bootstrap working without the number in public.

Next action: confirm `fleet` (or name it yourself) and say whether items 1–5 are the right set — then I'll create the repo, move them, and wire the input.

content.text:
Consolidated plan. Private repo **`sauyon/dotfiles-private`**, added as a `flake = false` input (like `mattpocock-skills`), holding four files:

1. **`identity.nix`** — git `user.email` and `signing.key` (`home.nix:3867,3874`), plus `user.name` unless you'd rather keep that. Caveat: every commit's metadata still carries the address, so this removes it from the *file*, not from history or future commits — worth it only as part of the general rule, which is why your CLAUDE.md carved it out in the first place.
2. **`newtab-links.nix`** — the 24-entry Work/Infra/Other link list (`home.nix:1622-1650`). Personal by definition, and the Infra group is internal URLs.
3. **`endpoints.nix`** — `wifAudience` (project number, pool, provider), `UNIFI_LOCAL_HOST`, the classifier endpoint in `local-auto-mode/config.py`, and the LAN address in the comment at `home.nix:2219`.

python3 <<'PY'
import re

# ---------- flake.nix ----------
f = open("flake.nix").read()
anchor = '    ssh-oidc.url = "git+https://codeberg.org/sauyon/ssh-oidc";'
assert anchor in f
f = f.replace(anchor, anchor + '''
    # Private companion to this repo: the git identity, internal endpoints,
    # the new-tab links and the per-host posture home.nix hands the Claude
    # auto-mode classifier. Not a flake -- a plain tree of nix values, like
    # mattpocock-skills above. It is private because a public repo is the
    # wrong place to MAINTAIN values that are of no use to anyone else;
    # credentials are a different problem and stay in secrets.yaml under KMS.
    # Needed at eval time, so a host must be able to read it: locally that is
    # git-credential-fj (home.nix), in CI a netrc line from FORGE_TOKEN.
    dotfiles-private.url = "git+https://forge.ko.ag/sauyon/dotfiles-private.git";
    dotfiles-private.flake = false;''', 1)

old_out = "  outputs = { nixpkgs, home-manager, nix-darwin, sops-nix, walker, nixgl, explore-mcp, drovr, hunk, mattpocock-skills, zen-browser, ssh-oidc, ... }:"
assert old_out in f, "outputs signature not found"
f = f.replace(old_out, old_out.replace(", ssh-oidc, ...", ", ssh-oidc, dotfiles-private, ..."), 1)

old_sa = "        inherit sops-nix walker nixgl explore-mcp drovr hunk mattpocock-skills zen-browser machine;"
assert old_sa in f, "extraSpecialArgs not found"
f = f.replace(old_sa, "        inherit sops-nix walker nixgl explore-mcp drovr hunk mattpocock-skills zen-browser machine;\n        inherit dotfiles-private;", 1)
open("flake.nix", "w").write(f)

# ---------- home.nix ----------
h = open("home.nix").read()
h = h.replace("  mattpocock-skills,\n  zen-browser,\n  machine,", "  mattpocock-skills,\n  zen-browser,\n  dotfiles-private,\n  machine,", 1)

anchor = "  gpu = machine.gpu or null;"
assert anchor in h
h = h.replace(anchor, anchor + '''

  # Values the public repo deliberately does not carry: see the
  # `dotfiles-private` flake input for why each one is in there rather than
  # here. Imported once, used from `private.*` below.
  private = {
    identity = import "${dotfiles-private}/identity.nix";
    endpoints = import "${dotfiles-private}/endpoints.nix";
    newtabLinks = import "${dotfiles-private}/newtab-links.nix";
    claudeAutoModeEnvByHost =
      import "${dotfiles-private}/claude-auto-mode.nix" { inherit hostname; };
  };''', 1)

h = re.sub(r'wifAudience = "[^"]+";', "wifAudience = private.endpoints.wifAudience;", h, count=1)
h = re.sub(r'UNIFI_LOCAL_HOST = "[^"]+";', "UNIFI_LOCAL_HOST = private.endpoints.unifiHost;", h, count=1)
h = re.sub(r'user\.name = "[^"]+";', "user.name = private.identity.name;", h, count=1)
h = re.sub(r'user\.email = "[^"]+";', "user.email = private.identity.email;", h, count=1)
h = re.sub(r'(signing = \{\n(?:.*\n)*?\s*)key = "[^"]+";', r"\1key = private.identity.signingKey;", h, count=1)

# newtabLinks list -> the private import
lines = h.split("\n")
s = next(i for i, l in enumerate(lines) if l.startswith("  newtabLinks = ["))
e = next(i for i in range(s + 1, len(lines)) if lines[i] == "  ];")
lines[s:e + 1] = ["  newtabLinks = private.newtabLinks;"]
h = "\n".join(lines)

# the LAN address in the historical comment
h = h.replace("as 10.0.7.110, inside any sane \"my LAN\" range",
              "as that node's own address, inside any sane \"my LAN\" range", 1)

# config.py gains a substituted placeholder rather than a hardcoded endpoint
old_cfg = '''  home.file.".claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py".source =
    ./home/.claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py;'''
assert old_cfg in h
h = h.replace(old_cfg, '''  # Substituted rather than copied: the router's LAN address comes from the
  # private input, so the checked-in file carries a placeholder.
  home.file.".claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py".text =
    builtins.replaceStrings [ "@LOCAL_CLASSIFIER_URL@" ] [ private.endpoints.localClassifierUrl ]
      (builtins.readFile ./home/.claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py);''', 1)

# the per-host posture is appended to the public shared list again
h = h.replace("      environment = claudeAutoModeEnvShared;",
              "      environment = claudeAutoModeEnvShared ++ private.claudeAutoModeEnvByHost;", 1)
open("home.nix", "w").write(h)

# ---------- config.py ----------
c = open("home/.claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py").read()
c = re.sub(r'(LOCAL_CLASSIFIER_URL", ")[^"]+(")', r'\1@LOCAL_CLASSIFIER_URL@\2', c, count=1)
open("home/.claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py", "w").write(c)
print("patched flake.nix, home.nix, config.py")
PY
nix-instantiate --parse flake.nix >/dev/null && nix-instantiate --parse home.nix >/dev/null && echo "parse OK"
echo "--- remaining hardcoded values (should be none in home.nix) ---"
grep -nE '10\.0\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+|484956590837' home.nix home/.claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py | head
echo "--- wif script lines to fix next ---"
sed -n '30p' install/wif/revoke-kid.sh; sed -n '67p' install/wif/jwks-refresh-probe.sh

    # opencode-claude-memory reads/writes Claude Code's own memory store

python3 <<'PY'
w = open(".forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml").read()
anchor = "      - name: build home closures"
assert anchor in w
step = '''      # The flake now takes a private input (dotfiles-private), and nix fetches
      # git+https by shelling out to git -- not through its own HTTP client, so
      # the attic netrc above does nothing for it. Hand git a credential helper
      # that answers out of the environment: the token stays in the runner's
      # env, never in argv and never in a file on disk.
      # Do NOT echo $FORGE_TOKEN or enable `set -x` here.
      - name: authorise git against the private input
        env:
          FORGE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FORGE_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          set -eu
          git config --global credential."https://forge.ko.ag".username oauth2
          git config --global credential."https://forge.ko.ag".helper \\
            '!f() { test "$1" = get && printf "password=%s\\n" "$FORGE_TOKEN"; }; f'

'''
w = w.replace(anchor, step + anchor, 1)

# the build step needs the token in its own environment too, since the helper
# reads it at fetch time
old_build = """      - name: build home closures
        run: |"""
new_build = """      - name: build home closures
        env:
          FORGE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.FORGE_TOKEN }}
        run: |"""
assert old_build in w
w = w.replace(old_build, new_build, 1)
open(".forgejo/workflows/nix-home.yml", "w").write(w)
print("patched nix-home.yml")

d = open("docs/ci-nix-home.md").read()
d = d.rstrip("\n") + '''

## The private input

The flake takes `dotfiles-private` (`git+https://forge.ko.ag/sauyon/dotfiles-private.git`),
a non-flake tree holding the values the public repo deliberately does not carry:
the git identity, internal endpoints, the new-tab links and the per-host posture
for Claude Code's auto-mode classifier. It is needed at **eval** time, so no host
and no CI job can evaluate this flake without read access to it.

Locally that access is `git-credential-fj` (declared in `home.nix`), which is why
a fresh host must `fj login` before its first switch. In CI it is the repo secret
`FORGE_TOKEN`, a Forgejo token scoped to `read:repository`, handed to git as a
credential helper that answers from the environment.

**nix fetches `git+https` by shelling out to git**, so the attic `netrc-file`
does nothing for this input -- a netrc line is the wrong fix and looks like it
should work. If a run fails with an auth error against `forge.ko.ag`, check that
`FORGE_TOKEN` is set on the *build* step and not only on the step that configures
the helper; the helper is invoked by git at fetch time, inside `nix build`.
'''
open("docs/ci-nix-home.md", "w").write(d)
print("documented in docs/ci-nix-home.md")

input.command:
git add -A && git status --porcelain && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline master..HEAD
scrub: move what is nobody else's business into a private input

This repo is public, and a handful of the values it carries are of no use
to a reader while being quite useful to the wrong one. Encryption is the
wrong tool for them: they are not credentials, they are facts -- and a
fact that has to be decrypted at activation cannot be read at eval time,
which is when home.nix needs these.

So they move to `dotfiles-private`, a non-flake input alongside
mattpocock-skills:

  identity.nix         git user.name / user.email / signing key
  endpoints.nix        WIF audience, UniFi controller, litellm router,
                       ko.ag admin host
  newtab-links.nix     the new-tab link list (Work/Infra name internals)
  claude-auto-mode.nix per-host posture for the auto-mode classifier

these hosts, so the block is written by hand, and the half of it that says

+nowhere, so a *new* one cannot open an *existing* `login.keyring` — sealing over a

+passphrase must be **text**: the daemon reads it back with `PW="$(unseal)"` and
+pipes it to `--unlock`, and command substitution drops NUL bytes while `--unlock`

+the job**: sealing a new passphrase while leaving the old `login.keyring` gives the
+daemon a collection it cannot unlock, which is the prompt-loop this design exists
+to remove. The rest pin enrolling with nothing on stdin, a fresh passphrase per
+run, and the refusal naming the file while writing no seal files.

---
name: private-values-go-in-dotfiles-private
description: In the dotfiles repo, anything private — not just emails — belongs in the dotfiles-private flake input, not the public tree.
metadata:

---

The dotfiles repo is public. Any value that is *nobody else's business* —
personal identifiers, the git identity, internal endpoints and LAN addresses,
per-host posture (which machines are work-issued, which hold live credentials),
personal link lists — goes in the private `dotfiles-private` flake input
(`git+https://forge.ko.ag/sauyon/dotfiles-private.git`, `flake = false`), which
`home.nix` imports as `private.*`. Credentials are a separate problem and stay
in `secrets.yaml` under GCP KMS.

**Why:** the user's stated rule is broader than the repo's written NO EMAILS
section — "anything private like emails or things should go in there". Encryption
is the wrong tool for non-secret private facts, because sops decrypts at

    # user.keystore behind and then passes the guard.
    stores() {
      ${pkgs.findutils}/bin/find "$KEYRINGS" -maxdepth 1 \
        \( -name '*.keyring' -o -name 'user.keystore' \) -printf '%f\n' 2>/dev/null || true
    }

    EXISTING="$(stores)"
    if [ "$FORCE" -eq 0 ] && [ -n "$EXISTING" ]; then
      echo "gnome-keyring-tpm-seal: $KEYRINGS already holds:" >&2
      printf '    %s\n' $EXISTING >&2
      echo "  A freshly generated passphrase cannot open any of them, so sealing now" >&2
      echo "  would lose every secret they hold. Enrolment is once per keyring, not" >&2
      echo "  once per boot." >&2
      echo "  If the TPM was cleared they are already unreadable, so nothing is lost by" >&2
      echo "  starting over: run with --force, which seals and then moves all of them" >&2
      echo "  aside, and sign back in to whatever stored secrets there (Bitwarden, the" >&2
      echo "  git credential helper). Then: systemctl --user restart gnome-keyring" >&2
      exit 1
    fi

    WORK="$(${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/mktemp -d "$RUN/gnome-keyring-seal.XXXXXX")"
    trap '${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT
    ${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/mkdir -p -m700 "$SEAL"

    # Generated here, per host, and never written anywhere but the TPM-sealed blob.
    # It used to be escrowed in secrets.yaml and piped in on stdin, which made the
    # "useless off this machine" claim above false -- one KMS-decryptable value
    # opened every host's keyring file -- and made a new host wait on a decrypt it
    # could not do. Nothing needs to know this value: the daemon unseals it, and a
    # TPM clear means starting the keyring over, which costs a few sign-ins.
    # base64, not raw bytes. The consumer is gnome-keyring-tpm above, which reads
    # the unsealed value with PW="$(unseal)" and pipes it with printf: command
    # substitution drops NUL bytes and strips trailing newlines, and --unlock reads
    # a newline-terminated password. Raw /dev/urandom would therefore hand the
    # keyring a *shorter* passphrase than was sealed for about a fifth of
    # enrolments, and an empty one when the first byte is 0x0a -- silently, since

content.content:
git-credential-fj = pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "git-credential-fj" ''
    set -euo pipefail

    # Only `get` is ours to answer — fj owns store/erase.
    [ "''${1:-}" = "get" ] || exit 0

    host=""
    while IFS='=' read -r key value; do
      [ -n "$key" ] || break
      case "$key" in
        host) host="$value" ;;
      esac
    done
    [ -n "$host" ] || exit 0

    keys="''${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/forgejo-cli/keys.json"
    [ -r "$keys" ] || exit 0

    # expires_at is time::OffsetDateTime's serde tuple, in order:
    # [year, day-of-year, hour, minute, second, nanos, offset-h, offset-m,
    # offset-s]. jq's mktime wants [year, month0, mday, h, m, s, wday, yday]
    # and is UTC-based, so build January 1st and add the ordinal by hand.
    # `-e` makes "still valid" exit 0; anything else — expired, absent
    # (Application login or unknown host), or unparseable — exits nonzero.
    if ! ${lib.getExe pkgs.jq} -e --arg h "$host" '
      .hosts[$h].expires_at
      | if type == "array" and length >= 9 then
          ([.[0], 0, 1, .[2], .[3], .[4], 0, 0] | mktime)
            + (.[1] - 1) * 86400
            - (.[6] * 3600 + .[7] * 60 + .[8])
          > now
        else true end
    ' "$keys" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      # Best-effort: a failed refresh still falls through to whatever is on

Everything is in place and master hasn't moved since the rebase.

**State:**
- `FORGE_TOKEN` set on `sauyon/dotfiles` (HTTP 201; readback: `ATTIC_TOKEN, FORGE_TOKEN`). The payload and auth config were shredded; the token value was never printed.
- Branch `auto-mode-env` — 2 commits, 2 ahead / 0 behind `master` (`17897ce`), tree clean.

- Private repo `sauyon/dotfiles-private` pushed (`6af310d`), pinned in `flake.lock`.

One incidental finding worth knowing: the `fj` store's OAuth token had expired (1-hour lifetime, dead 3.5h) and `fj whoami` refreshed it. That's the same expiry behind your `hms` mid-poll 401s — anything reaching the forge needs a refresh immediately before use, not a snapshot taken earlier.

Merging is the one step I won't take on my own here. Say merge and I'll fast-forward `master` to `7842ed5` and run `hms` — that push is the first real test of the `FORGE_TOKEN` fetch path, and if CI fails there, `docs/ci-nix-home.md` now names the symptom and the fix.

Shipped and verified on this host.

**What landed** — `master` = `7842ed5`, CI run 121 green ([run](https://forge.ko.ag/sauyon/dotfiles/actions/runs/121)), switch was a pure download (0 KiB), exit 0.

**Verified after the switch, not assumed:**
- `~/.config/claude-personal/settings.json` → 11 `autoMode.environment` entries, last one shiori's posture line.
- `~/.claude/plugins/local-auto-mode/config.py` → zero occurrences of `@LOCAL_CLASSIFIER_URL@`; the real address substituted in.
- `git config` in the repo → `user.name`, `user.email`, `user.signingkey` all resolve from the private input.
- The `FORGE_TOKEN` path worked in CI on its first run — that was the assumption I flagged as untestable locally.

**The original problem** is closed by routing around it rather than fixing it: `/auto-mode-setup` still cannot save on any of these hosts, and now never needs to — the block is declarative, applies to all four profiles, and a reinstall keeps it.

Cleanup: merged worktree and branch removed, `install/wif` bootstrap scripts now require `KO_ADMIN_HOST` / `KO_WIF_AUDIENCE` (values in the private repo's README), and the measured one-hour `fj` token lifetime is recorded against your existing `hms` 401 note.

Two loose ends I did not touch, both yours to judge:
1. `tests/wif-tpm.sh` check 8 — *"the old file key can no longer mint an STS token"* — fails on master and did before this work. It says a superseded key can still mint tokens, which is worth chasing on its own.
2. The bentoml VPN on fujiwara is now written down as due for revocation, but only in the private repo — nothing revokes it.
